extracted.subtask_description: Official reviewer guidance for NeurIPS 2020 describing reviewer responsibilities, required review form fields, scoring conventions, confidentiality/double-blind rules, and best practices for producing constructive, reproducible, and fair reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsibilities (overall)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each reviewer will be assigned ~4-6 submissions and is responsible for reviewing submissions, reading author responses, discussing submissions and author responses with other reviewers and area chairs (ACs), and helping make decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Log into CMT promptly to check assignments and conflicts; if uncomfortable reviewing a paper, fill out a note in CMT and contact the AC immediately so an alternate reviewer can be found. Reviewer identities are visible to other reviewers, ACs and SACs; reviews and meta-reviews are made public after decisions (identities remain anonymous).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict of interest check
rubrics_metrics.description: As soon as reviewers are notified, they must log into CMT to check for conflicts and ensure papers fall within their expertise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep domain conflicts in CMT up to date. If you have a conflict or are not comfortable reviewing a paper, fill out a note in CMT and inform the AC immediately. Read what constitutes conflict of interest for NeurIPS 2020 (linked).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer availability and communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Respect deadlines and respond to emails promptly; inform ACs if you will be unavailable for important windows (e.g., discussion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most emails will come from CMT (email@msr-cmt.org); whitelist this address and check spam. If changing email address, update CMT. Never reply directly to CMT emails; use CMT 'email meta-reviewer' links.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer evaluation by ACs (meta-review scoring of reviewers)
rubrics_metrics.description: ACs will evaluate the quality of each review using three scores: 'exceeded expectations', 'met expectations', and 'failed to meet expectations'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Top 8% of reviewers (highest scores) will be awarded free registrations; top 30% will have registrations reserved; lowest-scoring reviewers may not be invited in the future. Write thoughtful, constructive reviews to meet expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professionalism, conduct, and Code of Conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviews must accord with the NeurIPS code of conduct and be professional and polite; avoid discriminatory language or subtle discrimination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid comments that imply authors are 'foreign' or 'non-native' (e.g., don't say 'have a native English speaker proofread'); prefer neutral phrasing like 'proof-read for English style and grammar issues.' Do not reveal identities if accidentally discovered. Agree to abide by the code of conduct (field in review form).

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep everything relating to the review process confidential; do not use ideas, code, or results from submissions in your own work until they become publicly available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not distribute submissions (code or ideas) without approval from program chairs. Code submitted for review cannot be distributed. Do not talk about or distribute submissions to anyone without prior approval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double-blind reviewing rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewing is double-blind at the level of reviewers and ACs (they cannot see author identities). Authors are responsible for anonymizing submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should not include names, affiliations, acknowledgements, or other identifying information (including in supplementary material). If a submission is not adequately anonymized, contact the corresponding AC. Do not attempt to de-anonymize authors (e.g., via Google or arXiv); if you accidentally learn identities, do not divulge them and do not let it influence your decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplementary material policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors may submit up to 100MB of supplementary material (PDF or ZIP). The reviewer's responsibility is to read and review the submission itself; reviewing supplementary material is discretionary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because NeurIPS submissions are short, reviewers may wish to consult supplementary material before criticizing a submission for missing details, proofs, or experimental results. Supplementary material can include proofs, derivations, data, or source code.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executing submitted code and clicking links (security)
rubrics_metrics.description: Submitted source code and web links may contain security vulnerabilities; exercise caution when executing code or visiting links.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If running supplementary source code, do so in a secure environment (recommended: Docker container, VM image such as VirtualBox/VMWare, or network-isolated cloud instance). Be cautious about accessing web links that may log IP addresses or contain vulnerabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formatting and page limit compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Submissions are limited to eight content pages (including figures/tables) in the NeurIPS 'submission' style; additional pages allowed only for (a) broader impact discussion and (b) references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors must use the NeurIPS 2020 LaTeX style file. If assigned submissions violate style (e.g., reduced margins or font size) or page limits, notify the AC immediately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dual submission policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Submissions that are identical or substantially similar to papers in other archival venues (or other NeurIPS submissions) should be deemed dual submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Slicing contributions too thinly may count as dual submission. If you suspect a dual submission, contact the corresponding AC. See Call for Papers and FAQ for more info.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review content — principle of detail and usefulness
rubrics_metrics.description: Review content is the primary means for ACs/SACs to make decisions and for authors to understand outcomes; reviews should be detailed and informative rather than short, superficial opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short, uninformed, or dismissive reviews are worse than no review. Reviews for rejected submissions should help authors improve; reviews for accepted submissions should help with camera-ready improvements. Include arguments for and against acceptance to help ACs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review field: Summary and contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: Briefly summarize the paper motivation, key contributions and achievements in a paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This helps ACs and authors detect misunderstandings. Contributions can be theoretical, methodological, algorithmic, empirical, bridge papers, or critical analyses. See Examples of Review Content for exemplar phrasings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review field: Strengths
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe the strengths of the work along axes like soundness, significance, novelty, and relevance to the NeurIPS community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List strengths concretely (e.g., sound theoretical claims, solid empirical methodology, significance relative to prior work) and cite precise prior work if claiming novelty or significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review field: Weaknesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain the limitations of the work along the same axes as strengths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide detailed, specific, and polite criticisms. Avoid vague, subjective complaints. Do not review based on personal interest; focus on scientific contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review field: Correctness
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether claims and methods are correct and whether empirical methodology is correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorrect claims or methodology are primary reasons for rejection. Provide detailed, specific, and polite explanations of any problems and motivate criticisms thoroughly so authors can respond.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review field: Clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Rate the clarity of exposition and indicate parts needing revision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give concrete examples of unclear sections or suggestions for reorganization, notation improvements, or missing explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review field: Relation to prior work
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the submission clearly discusses how it differs from previous contributions and properly situates itself in the literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Related work should not be a mere list; it should explain differences. Authors are excused for not knowing very recent non-refereed work (arXiv < 2 months before deadline is considered contemporaneous). Cite prior work precisely where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review field: Reproducibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge whether there are enough details to reproduce the major results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If not reproducible, list lack of reproducibility among weaknesses. Consider suggesting what additional details would be needed to reproduce results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review field: Additional feedback and questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide any other comments, suggestions for improvement, and questions for the authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this field for requests for clarification (e.g., 'I would like to see results of experiment X' or 'Please include parameter settings for experiment Y'). Be specific so authors can address in the author response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall score (10–1) guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Overall Score should reflect your assessment of the submission’s contributions and not be adjusted to match conference acceptance rates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scores mapping: 10=Top 5% of accepted papers (groundbreaking); 9=Top 15% (excellent); 8=Top 50% (very good); 7=Good accept; 6=Marginally above threshold; 5=Marginally below threshold; 4=Okay but not good enough; 3=Clear reject; 2=Strong reject (surprised it was submitted); 1=Trivial/wrong/already known. Provide justification in review text; do not assume your assignment is representative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidence score guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Rate your confidence (5–1) in your assessment reflecting familiarity with the work and related literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 5=absolutely certain; 4=confident but not absolute; 3=fairly confident; 2=willing to defend but likely gaps; 1=educated guess/not in area. Use this to communicate how much your score should be trusted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broader impact statement adequacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicate whether the authors have adequately addressed broader impacts, including potential negative ethical and societal implications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors are required to include a broader impact statement discussing both positive and negative outcomes. Mark Yes/No/Only partially and provide explanation to give balanced perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential ethical concerns flag
rubrics_metrics.description: Flag whether the submission raises potential ethical concerns (methods, applications, or data that create/reinforce unfair bias or aim at harm).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Answer Yes/No and briefly explain if concerns exist. This rating is independent of acceptance; if AC shares the concern, dedicated ethics reviewers may be assigned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Previous reviewing of the work
rubrics_metrics.description: Declare whether you have previously reviewed or area chaired a version of this work for another archival venue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Yes/No; this helps ACs/SACs contextualize your review. ACs have access to resubmission statements from authors describing prior submissions and changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidential comments to area chair
rubrics_metrics.description: Optional confidential field for comments to the AC that are not shown to authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use for blunt criticisms, explicit comparisons to other submissions, or context you prefer the authors not see. Be careful with identity revelations; do not disclose author identities even if accidentally learned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author response handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers must read author responses and, if appropriate, update their reviews; ignoring author responses is unfair.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reading author responses, keep an open mind. Update the review to indicate you read the response and whether you agree or disagree with it; be more specific than 'I have read the author response and my opinion remains the same'—explain why.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discussion phase engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: After author response, the AC will initiate discussion to reach reviewer consensus; reviewers should engage actively in these discussions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discussion is important for borderline or conflicting assessments. Consider other reviewers' perspectives and change your mind if appropriate, but you are not required to. Consensus is valuable but not mandatory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of acceptable contributions and review text (exemplars)
rubrics_metrics.description: The guidelines provide example phrasings and exemplar review excerpts illustrating contributions (theoretical, empirical, bridging fields), quality checks, clarity comments, originality, and significance assessments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use exemplar language as a model (e.g., describe empirical validation, computational complexity advantages, robustness claims). Examples show how to structure pros/cons, point out technical issues precisely, and suggest concrete improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling of non-anonymized submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: If a submission assigned to you is not adequately anonymized (contains author names/affiliations/acknowledgements/other identifying information), you should contact the corresponding AC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attempt to discover author identities yourself; do not let any accidentally discovered identity influence your review; document the problem to the AC.
